entries.lesson_core_move: Test Fourier-integral convergence for continuous-time signals and LTI impulse responses to recognize when frequency-response analysis on the \(j\omega\) axis must be extended with Laplace-domain exponential weighting.

sections.section_title: Testing Convergence for a Decaying Time Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=e^{-3|t|}$, determine whether the Fourier transform exists on the $j\omega$ axis. Use the same core move as the step example: test absolute convergence of the transform integral.

choice_blocks.text: $|e^{-3|t|}e^{-j\omega t}|=e^{-3|t|}$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-3|t|}dt=\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{3t}dt+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-3t}dt=\frac{2}{3}<\infty$ and therefore $X(j\omega)$ is valid.
The signal is bounded, so boundedness alone is sufficient; no integral test is needed.
The transform can only converge at $\omega=0$, where the oscillatory factor is absent and cancellation is strongest.
Because this is two-sided, one side must diverge and force failure regardless of what the other side does.
The absolute-integrability test is not required; one-sided support is the only condition for convergence on $j\omega$.

questions.correct_answer: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|dt<\infty$, and for $x(t)=e^{-3|t|}$ the integral is finite, so $X(j\omega)$ exists.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Take magnitude first: the oscillatory factor disappears and $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$. The two one-sided pieces integrate to finite values, so the absolute integral is finite and the Fourier transform exists on $j\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=e^{-4|t|}$, identify the correct conclusion from the Fourier-convergence test.

choice_blocks.text: Split both halves: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|e^{-4|t|}|dt=\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{4t}dt+\int_0^{\infty}e^{-4t}dt=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{1}{2}<\infty$, so $X(j\omega)$ exists.
Check only boundedness: since $|x(t)|\le1$, the Fourier transform is valid only for a finite set of frequencies.
Growth on the left side dominates even though it decays, so the bilateral integral is divergent.
Checking only $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-4t}dt$ is enough; ignore the negative-time side.
Even with decay on one side, one-sided exponentials always require Laplace-weighting first.

questions.correct_answer: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|dt=\frac{1}{2}<\infty$, so the Fourier transform on $j\omega$ is valid for this decaying two-sided signal.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Again, the oscillatory term has unit magnitude. The split at $t=0$ yields two finite improper integrals, so the absolute integral is finite and the transform exists on the $j\omega$ axis.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Divergence for a Nondecaying Time Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=3$, determine whether a frequency-response $X(j\omega)$ exists. Use the same core move as the example and test absolute convergence.

choice_blocks.text: $|3e^{-j\omega t}|=3$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}3\,dt=\infty$. The absolute integral does not converge, so $X(j\omega)$ does not exist.
The integral over any finite window is finite, so this is enough to claim $X(j\omega)$ exists.
The signal is bounded, therefore boundedness is sufficient for Fourier-transform existence for all frequencies.
Because the exponential kernel oscillates, the improper integral always converges by cancellation.
$X(j\omega)$ exists only when $\omega\neq 0$ so that oscillatory cancellation is strongest.

questions.correct_answer: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|dt=\infty$, so the Fourier integral is not absolutely convergent and $X(j\omega)$ is not defined in the ordinary sense.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Taking magnitude removes the phase term: $|3e^{-j\omega t}|=3$. The resulting time integral has infinite area on $(-\infty,\infty)$, so this is a clean divergence case and the Fourier transform is not valid on the $j\omega$ axis.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=u(t-1)$, choose the correct conclusion about $X(j\omega)$.

choice_blocks.text: $|u(t-1)e^{-j\omega t}|=u(t-1)$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(t-1)\,dt=\int_{1}^{\infty}1\,dt=\infty$ and $X(j\omega)$ does not exist.
The signal has one-sided support, so one-sided support always guarantees convergence on $j\omega$.
Because $x(t)$ is bounded by 1, boundedness alone confirms a valid Fourier transform.
The shift changes the signal support but does not affect convergence, so $X(j\omega)$ converges only for $\omega\neq 0$.
Cancellation from $e^{-j\omega t}$ makes the improper integral conditionally convergent for all finite $\omega$.

questions.correct_answer: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|x(t)|dt=\int_{1}^{\infty}1\,dt=\infty$, so the Fourier transform does not exist in the ordinary sense.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t-1)$, absolute convergence still uses $|x(t)e^{-j\omega t}|=|x(t)|=u(t-1)$. The integral over the nonzero tail from $1$ to $\infty$ diverges, so this one-sided but nondecaying signal also fails the same test.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Divergence for a Growing Exponential Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=e^{4t}u(t)$, choose the correct conclusion about $X(j\omega)$.

choice_blocks.text: Because $\left|e^{4t}u(t)e^{-j\omega t}\right|=e^{4t}u(t)$, the absolute integral is $\int_0^{\infty}e^{4t}\,dt=\infty$, so $X(j\omega)$ does not exist and a weighted (Laplace-domain) form is needed.
The Fourier factor $e^{-j\omega t}$ is oscillatory, so the integral must be conditionally convergent for every finite $\omega$.
Because the signal is one-sided ($t\ge0$), causal support alone guarantees Fourier-transform existence.
The absolute integral converges when $\omega\neq0$ because oscillatory cancellation is strongest off the origin.
A phase-only rewrite of $e^{4t}$ into the complex kernel makes the exponential growth harmless, so $X(j\omega)$ exists.

questions.correct_answer: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|e^{4t}u(t)e^{-j\omega t}|\,dt=\int_0^{\infty}e^{4t}\,dt=\infty$, so $X(j\omega)$ does not exist in the ordinary Fourier sense.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude step removes $e^{-j\omega t}$. For a one-sided growing exponential, the absolute integral is over $[0,\infty)$ and diverges, so the standard Fourier transform test fails.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(-t)$, test convergence on the $j\omega$ axis and choose the correct conclusion.

choice_blocks.text: For $t\le0$, $\left|e^{-3t}\right|$ grows as $t\to-\infty$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-3t}u(-t)\,dt=\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-3t}\,dt=\infty$ and no $X(j\omega)$ exists.
The signal is one-sided (left-sided), so one-sided support is a sufficient condition for Fourier-transform existence.
Because $\left|e^{-j\omega t}\right|=1$, the two-sided Fourier integral converges as long as $\omega\neq0$.
The anti-causal support guarantees exponential attenuation in magnitude, so the absolute integral is automatically finite.
This is a valid Fourier-transform case because the signal is bounded by $1$ for all $t$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The absolute integrability check is unchanged by the sign of support. On $(-\infty,0]$, the envelope still grows exponentially, so the improper one-sided integral diverges and $X(j\omega)$ is not defined in the ordinary Fourier sense.

sections.section_title: Testing Whether an Impulse Response Has a Frequency Response

prompt_blocks.text: Test whether the impulse response $h(t)=\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}u(t)$ has a valid Fourier-domain frequency response. Use the same absolute-integrability rule as in this lesson.
Select the best conclusion from the options.

choice_blocks.text: No frequency response, because $\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}\,dt$ diverges as $\ln(1+t)$.
Yes, because $\int_0^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}\,dt=1<\infty$, so $H(j\omega)$ exists in the ordinary Fourier sense.
No, because one-sided support automatically means the Fourier integral must diverge.
No, because the function can be written in a Laplace-like form, so the Fourier transform is not needed.
Yes, because $h(t)$ is nonnegative so $\int |h(t)|dt$ must be finite.

questions.correct_answer: $h(t)=\frac{1}{(1+t)^2}u(t)$ does have a Fourier-domain frequency response since $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|\,dt=1<\infty$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The absolute integral is finite, so the Fourier-transform integral is absolutely convergent and $H(j\omega)$ exists. The side length of support does not replace this direct absolute-area test.

prompt_blocks.text: Test whether $h(t)=2e^{2t}u(-t)$ has a valid frequency response on the $j\omega$ axis.
Pick the best answer.

choice_blocks.text: No, because the exponent is positive and therefore the response cannot be Fourier-transformable.
Yes, because $\int_{-\infty}^{0}2e^{2t}\,dt=1<\infty$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|dt$ is finite.
No, because anti-causal signals never have Fourier-domain frequency responses.
Yes, because any function that decays on one side has a valid Fourier transform automatically.
No, because the response is defined using a unit step, and unit-step support always forces divergence.

questions.correct_answer: $h(t)=2e^{2t}u(-t)$ has a valid Fourier-domain frequency response because the absolute envelope is integrable over negative time and gives a finite value.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the same criterion as this step: test $\int |h(t)|dt$. Since $h(t)$ is nonzero only for $t\le 0$,
The absolute integral is finite, so the Fourier transform of $h(t)$ on the $j\omega$ axis exists even though the exponential is anti-causal.

sections.section_title: Deciding When Laplace-Domain Weighting Is Needed

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, decide the transform decision and the condition on $\sigma$ required to make the weighted form converge.

choice_blocks.text: Fourier does not converge because $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{3t}\,dt=\infty$, and the weighted integral is finite only when $\sigma>3$.
Fourier converges because $e^{-j\omega t}$ provides cancellation, and weighted convergence needs only $\sigma<3$.
Fourier converges for $\omega\neq 0$, and weighted convergence is automatic for any nonzero $\sigma$.
Weighted convergence requires $\sigma<3$, but Fourier convergence is also valid at $\sigma=0$ if $\omega\neq 0$.
Once any $\sigma$ is chosen, the one-sided integral converges because the support is causal.

questions.correct_answer: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, the unweighted Fourier integral diverges and does not exist on the $j\omega$ axis; weighted form converges only when $\sigma>3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First test the Fourier case: with $\sigma=0$, $\int_0^\infty e^{3t}\,dt=\infty$, so $X(j\omega)$ is not valid. With weighting, the magnitude envelope is $e^{(3-\sigma)t}$ on $[0,\infty)$, so convergence requires $\sigma>3$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(-t)$, choose the correct step-level decision about Fourier validity and weighted Laplace requirement.
Evaluate the same sign rule carefully on the anti-causal support interval $t\le 0$.

choice_blocks.text: Fourier converges because the signal decays as $t\to-\infty$ and already gives $\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{2t}\,dt=\frac12$, so no weighting is needed; if weighted, absolute convergence is kept for $\sigma<2$.
Fourier never converges because $e^{2t}$ grows on the left side, so weighted form is needed for any $\sigma>0$.
Weighted convergence is valid only for $\sigma>2$, which is the same rule as the causal case.
Any anti-causal signal is automatically unsuitable for Fourier analysis unless the signal is multiplied by a unit-step window.
The choice $\sigma=0$ is always required whenever a signal is anti-causal; other $\sigma$ values are irrelevant.

questions.correct_answer: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(-t)$, Fourier on the $j\omega$ axis already exists because the signal decays on $t\to-\infty$, so $\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{2t}dt=\frac12$ is finite; the weighted integral remains convergent for $\sigma<2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The anti-causal support is $t\le0$, so this is not the same sign rule as the causal-growth case. For $\sigma=0$, $\int_{-\infty}^0 e^{2t}\,dt$ is finite, so Fourier is valid here. Introducing $e^{-\sigma t}$ changes the exponent to $(2-\sigma)t$ on $(-\infty,0]$, which converges only when $\sigma<2$.

entries.lesson_title: Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether a continuous-time signal lacks a convergent Fourier transform by testing the Fourier-transform integral for convergence and interpreting nondecaying or growing behavior as requiring Laplace-domain exponential weighting.

sections.lesson_title: Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
sections.section_title: Testing Fourier-Transform Integral Convergence

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, which statement correctly tests whether the Fourier-transform integral $X(j\omega)=\int_0^\infty e^{-3t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ converges?

choice_blocks.text: It converges because $\int_0^\infty |e^{-3t}e^{-j\omega t}|\,dt=\int_0^\infty e^{-3t}\,dt=\frac{1}{3}$.
It diverges because the factor $e^{-j\omega t}$ keeps oscillating as $t\to\infty$.
It converges only after checking $\int_{-\infty}^0 e^{-3t}\,dt$, since $u(t)$ selects negative time.
It diverges because $|e^{-j\omega t}|=|\omega|$, so the envelope is $|\omega|e^{-3t}$.
It diverges because every one-sided exponential has a nonzero boundary term at $t=0$.

questions.correct_answer: The Fourier-transform integral converges because the absolute-value integral is finite: $\int_0^\infty e^{-3t}\,dt=\frac{1}{3}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The complex kernel has unit magnitude, so the convergence test uses the envelope $e^{-3t}$.
Because this improper integral is finite, the Fourier-transform integral converges.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{at}u(t)$ with real $a$, which condition on $a$ makes the Fourier-transform integral $X(j\omega)=\int_0^\infty e^{at}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ converge?

choice_blocks.text: $a<0$, because then $\int_0^\infty e^{at}\,dt$ is finite.
$a>0$, because a positive exponent cancels the oscillation in $e^{-j\omega t}$.
$a=0$, because the kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ has magnitude $1$.
$a\le 0$, because zero decay is enough when the phase factor is present.
All real $a$, because the Fourier-transform kernel always guarantees convergence.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Since $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$, absolute convergence is controlled by $\int_0^\infty e^{at}\,dt$.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: \int_0^\infty e^{at}\,dt \text{ is finite exactly when } a<0

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $a=0$ the envelope is constant, and for $a>0$ it grows, so neither case gives a convergent Fourier-transform integral.

sections.lesson_title: Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
sections.section_title: Recognizing Nondecaying Signals That Do Not Converge

prompt_blocks.text: For the ordinary Fourier-transform improper integral over $(-\infty,\infty)$, classify the signal $x(t)=1$.

choice_blocks.text: It does not converge, because the signal does not decay on either tail.
It converges because $x(t)$ is bounded for all $t$.
It converges because $e^{-j\omega t}$ decays as $|t|$ grows.
It converges because checking one tail is enough for a two-sided Fourier integral.
It converges in the standard improper-integral sense because the transform can be interpreted using impulses.

questions.correct_answer: It does not converge, because $x(t)=1$ has nondecaying tails over $(-\infty,\infty)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The Fourier kernel has unit magnitude, so it does not make the constant signal shrink on the tails.
Because the signal has infinite area over the unbounded time axis, the ordinary Fourier-transform integral does not converge.

prompt_blocks.text: For the ordinary Fourier-transform improper integral over $(-\infty,\infty)$, classify the signal $x(t)=1+0.1\cos(\omega_0 t)$.

choice_blocks.text: It converges because the oscillating term has positive and negative swings.
It does not converge, because the signal remains nondecaying on the unbounded interval.
It converges because every bounded periodic signal has a standard Fourier integral.
It converges after checking only the behavior as $t\to\infty$.
It converges in the ordinary improper-integral sense because distributional impulses can represent periodic components.

questions.correct_answer: It does not converge, because $x(t)=1+0.1\cos(\omega_0 t)$ stays nondecaying over $(-\infty,\infty)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The added cosine does not create decay, and the DC offset keeps the magnitude bounded away from zero.
A nondecaying signal over an unbounded interval fails the standard Fourier convergence test, even though engineering conventions may describe related distributional transforms separately.

sections.lesson_title: Signals Whose Fourier Transform Does Not Converge
sections.section_title: Recognizing Growing Signals That Do Not Converge

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{5t}u(t)$, what happens to the ordinary Fourier-transform integral $X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$?

choice_blocks.text: It does not converge, because on $t\ge 0$ the magnitude behaves like $e^{5t}$ and $\int_0^\infty e^{5t}\,dt=\infty$.
It converges because the factor $e^{-j\omega t}$ oscillates and therefore cancels the growth of $e^{5t}$.
It converges because every right-sided exponential $e^{at}u(t)$ has a Fourier transform when $a>0$.
It converges for all real $\omega$ without needing to check the sign of the exponential rate.
It should be tested on $t<0$ as $\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{5t}\,dt$, so the Fourier transform converges.

questions.correct_answer: It does not converge because the right-sided tail grows: $\int_0^\infty e^{5t}\,dt=\infty$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The unit step restricts the signal to $t\ge 0$, and the Fourier kernel has unit magnitude. The convergence test is controlled by the growing factor $e^{5t}$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(-t)$, which classification is correct for the ordinary Fourier-transform integral?

choice_blocks.text: It does not converge, because on $t\le 0$ the magnitude grows as $t\to -\infty$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-2t}\,dt=\infty$.
It converges because the exponent $-2$ is negative, so $e^{-2t}$ must decay on any one-sided support.
It converges because $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$ means the Fourier kernel supplies the needed damping.
It converges for every real $\omega$ without checking which side of the time axis contains the tail.
It should be treated like $e^{-2t}u(t)$ on $t\ge 0$, so $\int_0^\infty e^{-2t}\,dt$ shows convergence.

questions.correct_answer: It does not converge because the left-sided tail grows as $t\to -\infty$: $\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-2t}\,dt=\infty$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support is $t\le 0$, not $t\ge 0$. On that left-sided tail, $e^{-2t}$ grows without bound as $t\to -\infty$, while $e^{-j\omega t}$ still has unit magnitude.

sections.section_title: Identifying Signals That Need Exponential Weighting

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, what condition on $\sigma$ makes $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(3-\sigma)t}\,dt$ finite?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>3$
$\sigma<3$
$\sigma\ge 3$
$|\sigma|<3$
$\omega>3$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The weighted tail has exponent $3-\sigma$. The one-sided improper integral $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(3-\sigma)t}\,dt$ converges only when $3-\sigma<0$, so $\sigma>3$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, what condition on $\sigma$ makes $\int_0^{\infty}e^{(-1-\sigma)t}\,dt$ finite?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>-1$
$\sigma<-1$
$\sigma\ge -1$
$|\sigma|<1$
$\omega>-1$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Convergence depends on the real exponent $-1-\sigma$, since $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$. The integral is finite only when $-1-\sigma<0$, which gives $\sigma>-1$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Apply exponential weighting to a continuous-time signal to determine how multiplying by \(e^{-\sigma t}\) can make a nonconvergent Fourier-transform integral converge and motivate the Laplace-domain variable \(s=\sigma+j\omega\).

sections.section_title: Applying a Decaying Weight to a Nondecaying Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=2u(t)$. For the weighted Fourier-style integral below, which condition on $\sigma$ makes it converge and what value does it equal?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>0$, with value $\dfrac{2}{\sigma+j\omega}$
No restriction on $\sigma$ is needed, with value $\dfrac{2}{\sigma+j\omega}$
$\sigma<0$, with value $\dfrac{2}{\sigma+j\omega}$
$\sigma>0$, with value $\dfrac{2}{\sigma-j\omega}$
$|\omega|<\sigma$, with value $\dfrac{2}{\sigma+j\omega}$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the exponential factors to get $2e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. The oscillatory factor has unit magnitude, so convergence on $[0,\infty)$ is controlled by $e^{-\sigma t}$, which requires $\sigma>0$.

prompt_blocks.text: Now use the same weighting idea for a left-sided step, $x(t)=u(-t)$. Which condition on $\sigma$ makes the integral converge, and what is the transformed form?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>0$, with value $\dfrac{1}{\sigma+j\omega}$
$\sigma<0$, with value $-\dfrac{1}{\sigma+j\omega}$
No restriction on $\sigma$ is needed, with value $-\dfrac{1}{\sigma+j\omega}$
$\sigma<0$, with value $\dfrac{1}{\sigma-j\omega}$
The integral diverges for every $\sigma$ because $u(-t)$ is nondecaying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The integrand is $e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. On $(-\infty,0]$, the magnitude is $e^{-\sigma t}$, so the tail as $t\to-\infty$ decays only when $\sigma<0$.

sections.section_title: Testing Convergence After Weighting

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, which condition and value correctly describe the weighted integral?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>-3$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma+3+j\omega}$.
$\sigma>3$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma-3+j\omega}$.
$\sigma<-3$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma+3+j\omega}$.
The integral converges only when $\omega>3$.
$\sigma>-3$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma-3+j\omega}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combining exponents gives $e^{-(\sigma+3+j\omega)t}$. The magnitude has real decay $e^{-(\sigma+3)t}$, so convergence requires $\sigma+3>0$, or $\sigma>-3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $a>0$ and $x(t)=e^{-at}u(t)$. Which answer gives the convergence condition and integral value?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>a$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma-a+j\omega}$.
$\sigma>-a$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma+a+j\omega}$.
$\sigma<-a$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma+a+j\omega}$.
The integral always diverges because $e^{-j\omega t}$ does not decay.
$\sigma>-a$, and the integral equals $\frac{1}{\sigma-a+j\omega}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The weighted integrand collapses to $e^{-(\sigma+a+j\omega)t}$. The oscillatory factor changes phase only, so the real-part test requires $\sigma+a>0$.

sections.section_title: Choosing a Larger Weight for a Growing Signal

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, determine the condition on $\sigma$ for $\int_0^{\infty}e^{3t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ to converge, and simplify the integral under that condition.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>3$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{\sigma-3+j\omega}$.
$\sigma<3$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{3-\sigma-j\omega}$.
$\sigma\ge 3$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{\sigma-3+j\omega}$.
No real value of $\sigma$ makes the integral converge.
$3-\sigma-j\omega<0$, so $\sigma>3-j\omega$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the exponentials so the integrand is $e^{(3-\sigma-j\omega)t}$. Only the real part controls one-sided convergence on $[0,\infty)$, so require $3-\sigma<0$, which gives $\sigma>3$.

prompt_blocks.text: For a fixed $a>0$, which condition and simplified value are correct for $\int_0^{\infty}e^{at}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>a$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{\sigma-a+j\omega}$.
$\sigma<a$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{a-\sigma-j\omega}$.
$\sigma\ge a$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{\sigma-a+j\omega}$.
$\sigma>a-j\omega$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{\sigma-a+j\omega}$.
$\sigma>a$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{a-\sigma-j\omega}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The combined exponent is $(a-\sigma-j\omega)t$. The imaginary term affects oscillation, but convergence depends on the real coefficient $a-\sigma$, so the strict condition is $a-\sigma<0$.

sections.section_title: Combining Exponential Weighting with the Fourier Kernel

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite the weighted Fourier-kernel integral $\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ using one compact $s$-domain kernel. Which expression and definition are correct?

choice_blocks.text: $\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=\sigma+j\omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=\sigma-j\omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=\omega-\sigma j$
$\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, with $s=\sigma+j\omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}y(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $\sigma=\omega+j$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the exponential factors by adding exponents: $e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. Therefore the compact kernel is $e^{-st}$ with $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: A one-sided weighted integral has kernel $e^{-a t}e^{-j\Omega t}$. Which choice rewrites $\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-a t}e^{-j\Omega t}\,dt$ in the form $\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-st}\,dt$?

choice_blocks.text: $\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=a-j\Omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=\Omega-aj$
$\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $s=a+j\Omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-a t}e^{-j\Omega t}\,dt$, with $s=a+j\Omega$
$\int_0^{\infty}z(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, with $a=\Omega+j$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The product $e^{-a t}e^{-j\Omega t}$ equals $e^{-(a+j\Omega)t}$. Matching that to $e^{-st}$ gives $s=a+j\Omega$, where $a$ is the real damping coordinate and $\Omega$ is the oscillatory frequency coordinate.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert an exponentially weighted Fourier integral into Laplace-domain notation by identifying \(s=\sigma+j\omega\), with \(\sigma\) setting the convergence-producing exponential weight and \(\omega\) setting the sinusoidal frequency.

sections.section_title: Identifying \(\sigma\) and \(\omega\) in \(s=\sigma+j\omega\)

prompt_blocks.text: Given $s=-3+j5$, identify $\sigma$ and $\omega$ in $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma=-3,\;\omega=5$
$\sigma=5,\;\omega=-3$
$\sigma=3,\;\omega=5$
$\sigma=-3,\;\omega=0$
$\sigma=5,\;\omega=3$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the given value to $s=\sigma+j\omega$. The part not multiplied by $j$ is $\sigma$, and the coefficient of $j$ is $\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $s=4-j6$, identify $\sigma$ and $\omega$ in $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma=4,\;\omega=-6$
$\sigma=-6,\;\omega=4$
$\sigma=4,\;\omega=6$
$\sigma=-4,\;\omega=-6$
$\sigma=4,\;\omega=0$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the imaginary part so the value has the form $\sigma+j\omega$. Since $-j6=j(-6)$, the coefficient of $j$ is negative.

sections.section_title: Combining \(e^{-\sigma t}\) and \(e^{-j\omega t}\) into \(e^{-st}\)

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $e^{-5t}e^{-j2t}$ in $e^{-st}$ form and state $s$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{-5t}e^{-j2t}$, so it is not a single $e^{-st}$ term

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the exponents because the factors have the same variable $t$: $e^A e^B=e^{A+B}$.
Matching $e^{-(5+j2)t}$ to $e^{-st}$ gives $s=5+j2$.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $e^{3t}e^{-j6t}$ in $e^{-st}$ form and state $s$.

choice_blocks.text: $e^{3t}e^{-j6t}$, so no single $s$ can be stated

answer_explanation_blocks.text: First merge the exponents, then rewrite the result with a leading minus sign so it matches $e^{-st}$.
Therefore the combined expression has $s=-3+j6$.

sections.section_title: Rewriting an Exponentially Weighted Fourier Integral in Terms of \(s\)

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ in $s$-notation. Which choice correctly gives both the integral and the corresponding $s$?

questions.correct_answer: A. Since $e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-(2+j\omega)t}=e^{-st}$, the corresponding complex variable is $s=2+j\omega$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Combine the two exponential factors into one exponent. The real weighting factor $e^{-2t}$ gives $\sigma=2$, and the oscillating factor $e^{-j\omega t}$ keeps the imaginary part $j\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: Rewrite $\int_{0}^{\infty}y(t)e^{4t}e^{-j7t}\,dt$ in $s$-notation. Which choice correctly preserves the limits and identifies $s$?

questions.correct_answer: A. Here $e^{4t}=e^{-(-4)t}$, so $\sigma=-4$ and the frequency term $e^{-j7t}$ gives the imaginary part $j7$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the product to $e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-st}$. Because $e^{4t}$ has a positive exponent, it corresponds to $\sigma=-4$, not $\sigma=4$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Weighting and Frequency Roles of a Given \(s\)

prompt_blocks.text: For $s=2-j5$, choose the correct interpretation of the real exponential factor and oscillatory frequency component in $e^{-st}$.

choice_blocks.text: The real part gives decay as $e^{-2t}$, and $\omega=-5$ gives the oscillatory factor $e^{j5t}$.
The real part gives growth as $e^{2t}$, and $\omega=-5$ gives the oscillatory factor $e^{j5t}$.
$\omega=-5$ gives decay as $e^{-5t}$, and $2$ is the oscillatory frequency.
Both $2$ and $-5$ are independent oscillatory frequencies, so there is no exponential decay or growth.
Because $\sigma\ne 0$, there is no oscillation; the expression only decays as $e^{-2t}$.

questions.correct_answer: A. Since $s=2-j5=2+j(-5)$, $\sigma=2$ produces decay $e^{-2t}$ and $\omega=-5$ gives $e^{-j(-5)t}=e^{j5t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the value to $s=\sigma+j\omega$. Here $\sigma=2$ and $\omega=-5$.
A positive $\sigma$ makes the real exponential factor decay, while the imaginary part sets the oscillatory factor.

prompt_blocks.text: For $s=-3+j2$, which choice correctly describes the weighting and frequency roles in $e^{-st}$?

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma=-3$ gives growth as $e^{3t}$, and $\omega=2$ gives the oscillatory factor $e^{-j2t}$.
$\sigma=-3$ gives decay as $e^{-3t}$, and $\omega=2$ gives the oscillatory factor $e^{-j2t}$.
$\omega=2$ gives growth as $e^{2t}$, and $\sigma=-3$ is the oscillatory frequency.
Both $-3$ and $2$ are frequencies, so $e^{-st}$ has no real exponential weighting.
Because $\sigma\ne 0$, the imaginary part does not cause oscillation.

questions.correct_answer: A. Since $s=-3+j2$, $\sigma=-3$ gives $e^{-(-3)t}=e^{3t}$, and $\omega=2$ gives the oscillatory factor $e^{-j2t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Separate the real and imaginary parts: $\sigma=-3$ and $\omega=2$.
A negative $\sigma$ produces growth in $e^{-\sigma t}$, and $\omega$ sets the sinusoidal frequency factor.

entries.lesson_title: Laplace Transform as a Generalization of Fourier Transform
entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret \(X(s)\) as the Fourier transform of \(x(t)e^{-\sigma t}\), identifying the ordinary Fourier transform as the \(\sigma=0\) specialization when convergence permits.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform as a Generalization of Fourier Transform
sections.section_title: Rewriting \(X(s)\) as a Fourier Transform of \(x(t)e^{-\sigma t}\)

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, rewrite the transform as a Fourier-style integral in $\omega$ by substituting $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[e^{-2t}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[e^{-2t}u(t)e^{+\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[e^{-2t}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[e^{-2t}u(t)]e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}[e^{-2t}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{+j\omega t}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Substitute $s=\sigma+j\omega$, then split $e^{-(\sigma+j\omega)t}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$. Grouping the terms gives $x(t)e^{-\sigma t}=e^{-2t}u(t)e^{-\sigma t}$ as the Fourier-weighted signal.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(-t)$ and $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$, choose the correct expression after setting $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}[e^{3t}u(-t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}[e^{3t}u(-t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{+j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}[e^{-3t}u(-t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{3t}u(-t)e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$
$X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{0}[e^{3t}u(-t)]e^{-(\sigma-j\omega)t}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use $s=\sigma+j\omega$, so $e^{-st}=e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}$. For $u(-t)$ the integration range is $(-\infty,0]$, and the weighted signal is $x(t)e^{-\sigma t}=e^{3t}u(-t)e^{-\sigma t}$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform as a Generalization of Fourier Transform
sections.section_title: Recovering the Fourier Transform by Setting \(\sigma=0\)

prompt_blocks.text: Given the weighted-Laplace form $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, which expression is correct after setting $\sigma=0$?

choice_blocks.text: $X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\omega t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{+j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace $\sigma$ with $0$ and use $e^{0\cdot t}=1$. The result is exactly the Fourier-kernel form $\int x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, so $X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$.

prompt_blocks.text: Start from $X(s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-st}\,dt$ with $s=\sigma+j\omega$. Which statement correctly shows the checkpoint when the damping parameter is zero?

choice_blocks.text: $X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-0\cdot t}]e^{-j\omega t}\,dt=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\omega t}]e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\sigma t}]\,dt$
$X(-j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$
$X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}[x(t)e^{-\sigma t}]e^{-j\omega t}e^{-\sigma t}\,dt$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: From $s=\sigma+j\omega$, the step sets $\sigma=0$, so $s=j\omega$ and $e^{-st}=e^{-0\cdot t}e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-j\omega t}$. The weighted signal becomes $x(t)e^{0\cdot t}=x(t)$, so the Laplace slice is the Fourier transform $X(j\omega)$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform as a Generalization of Fourier Transform
sections.section_title: Comparing Weighted and Unweighted Transform Integrals

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which option gives the correct comparison between unweighted and weighted transforms?

choice_blocks.text: Use the unweighted Fourier form directly: $X(j\omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$; the Fourier integral already converges, so a positive damping factor is not required.
Use the weighted form with $\sigma>0$ for all $\sigma$: $X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{+\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt=\frac{1}{2-\sigma-j\omega}$.
The Fourier form is convergent only when $\omega\neq 0$, so the weighted form is the default choice.
Neither form is valid here because $u(t)$ makes the integral diverge on any side.
Use weighted and unweighted interchangeably: $X(j\omega)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-\omega t}\,dt$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ is decaying on $[0,\infty)$, the unweighted Fourier integral converges. The weighted form is still valid as a Laplace-style extension, but it is not required by convergence for this signal.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{2t}u(t)$, choose the option that correctly applies the convergence comparison step.

choice_blocks.text: The unweighted Fourier form converges and equals $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2-j\omega}$, so the weighted form should not be used.
The unweighted form diverges; the weighted form converges for any $\sigma>0$ and equals $\frac{1}{\sigma+2+j\omega}$.
Use $\sigma<2$ with $X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{(2-\sigma)t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$.
The unweighted Fourier form diverges; the weighted form converges only if $\sigma>2$, with $X(s)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{2t}e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt=\frac{1}{\sigma-2+j\omega}$.
The unweighted form diverges, but the weighted form is valid only when $\sigma=2$, which gives the limiting value $\frac{1}{j\omega}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A growing one-sided signal has $|e^{2t}e^{-j\omega t}|=e^{2t}$, so the unweighted integral diverges. Multiply by $e^{-\sigma t}$ first; the effective magnitude is $e^{(2-\sigma)t}$, so convergence requires $\sigma>2$.

sections.lesson_title: Laplace Transform as a Generalization of Fourier Transform
sections.section_title: Interpreting \(X(s)\) as a Family of Fourier Transforms Indexed by \(\sigma\)

prompt_blocks.text: From the worked example idea with $s=\sigma+j\omega$, choose the best interpretation of $X_{\sigma_1}(\omega)$ and $X_{\sigma_2}(\omega)$ for fixed $\omega$, defined as $X_{\sigma_i}(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(t)e^{-\sigma_i t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$.

choice_blocks.text: The two expressions are Fourier transforms of $u(t)e^{-\sigma_1 t}$ and $u(t)e^{-\sigma_2 t}$, so they are different members of one $\sigma$-indexed family that share the same frequency variable $\omega$.
All values of $\sigma$ are equivalent, so $X_{\sigma_1}(\omega)=X_{\sigma_2}(\omega)$ for any admissible pair.
Increasing $\sigma$ increases oscillation rate and decreases frequency content, so $\sigma$ is the frequency axis while $\omega$ is the damping term.
The correct family form replaces $u(t)e^{-\sigma_i t}$ with $\frac{1}{1+\sigma_i t}$, which yields the same integral shape with no change in variable roles.
The pair is one inverse Fourier transform and one Laplace transform because the two formulas use different signs in the exponential kernel.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The correct interpretation is that $\sigma$ controls exponential weighting of the same base signal and thus selects different members of the same Fourier-transform family at the same $\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ define $X_{\sigma}(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-\sigma t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$. Which statement correctly compares the two cases $\sigma_1=1$ and $\sigma_2=3$?

choice_blocks.text: $X_{\sigma_1}(\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-3t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and $X_{\sigma_2}(\omega)=\int_0^{\infty}e^{-5t}e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$, both valid as a stronger-damping family in the same Fourier-kernel form.
$\sigma$ is only a frequency shift, so both choices are equivalent to replacing $\omega$ by $\omega+\sigma$ in $X(j\omega)$.
$X_{\sigma_1}$ and $X_{\sigma_2}$ use the same weighted signal and differ only by the output frequency label, so damping does not change time-domain weighting.
For this signal, adding $e^{-\sigma t}$ does not change the weighted integral, so the two values are numerically equal when they both converge.
The only effect of changing $\sigma$ is replacing $e^{-\sigma t}$ with $\frac{1}{1+t}$ and keeping the same exponent magnitude.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $\sigma_1=1$, the weighted exponent is $e^{-3t}$, and for $\sigma_2=3$, it is $e^{-5t}$. Both are Fourier transforms of different weighted causal signals, so they are two members of the same $\sigma$-indexed family.

prompt_blocks.text: For the point $s=3-j2$ shown in the $s$-plane, which description is correct for the time-domain exponential weighting in $e^{-st}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $s=3-j2$ gives $\sigma=3$, so $e^{-st}=e^{-3t}e^{j2t}$. The negative real exponent means exponential decay; $\omega$ only controls oscillation frequency.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine the region of convergence by using exponential weighting to identify the set of \(s\)-plane values for which a signal's Laplace-transform integral converges.

sections.section_title: Testing Convergence at One \(s\)-Plane Value

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, test whether $X(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-3t}e^{-st}\,dt$ converges at $s=-2+j4$.

choice_blocks.text: Converges, because $\sigma=-2$ and $\sigma>-3$.
Diverges, because $\sigma=-2$ and $\sigma<-3$.
Diverges, because $|s|>3$ makes the exponential grow.
Converges conditionally but not absolutely, because $e^{-j4t}$ oscillates.
Diverges, because the test should use $\omega=4$ and $4>-3$.

questions.correct_answer: Converges, because substituting $s=-2+j4$ leaves the magnitude controlled by $e^{-t}$, so $\sigma=-2>-3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $e^{-j4t}$ has magnitude $1$, so convergence is controlled by $\int_0^{\infty}e^{-t}\,dt$, which is finite. Thus the transform converges at this $s$ value.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{t}u(t)$, test whether $X(s)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{t}e^{-st}\,dt$ converges at $s=j2$.

choice_blocks.text: Converges, because $\omega=2$ and the imaginary part creates oscillation.
Diverges, because $\sigma=0$ and the required condition is $\sigma>1$.
Converges, because $\sigma=0$ and $0>-1$.
Converges conditionally but not absolutely, because $e^{-j2t}$ oscillates.
Diverges only if $|s|<1$, so this point converges because $|j2|=2$.

questions.correct_answer: Diverges, because substituting $s=j2$ leaves the magnitude controlled by $e^{t}$, so $\sigma=0$ does not satisfy $\sigma>1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The oscillatory factor $e^{-j2t}$ has magnitude $1$, so the tail behaves like $\int_0^{\infty}e^{t}\,dt$, which is not finite. Therefore the Laplace transform diverges at $s=j2$.

sections.section_title: Converting a Convergence Test into a Condition on \(\sigma\)

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$, convert the convergence requirement into the inequality on $\sigma$ that defines the ROC for $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>-4$
$\sigma<-4$
$\sigma\ge -4$
$\omega>-4$
$\sigma>4$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The magnitude-relevant exponential is $e^{-4t}e^{-\sigma t}=e^{-(4+\sigma)t}$. The tail converges only when the exponent coefficient is negative, so $-(4+\sigma)<0$, which gives $\sigma>-4$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{3t}u(t)$, rewrite the convergence test as a condition on $\sigma$ for all $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

choice_blocks.text: $\sigma>3$
$\sigma<3$
$\sigma\ge 3$
$\omega>3$
$\sigma>-3$

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The product $e^{3t}e^{-st}$ has magnitude $e^{(3-\sigma)t}$ because $|e^{-j\omega t}|=1$. Convergence requires $3-\sigma<0$, so the ROC condition is $\sigma>3$.

sections.section_title: Checking Whether the Fourier-Transform Slice Is Included in the Region of Convergence

prompt_blocks.text: For a signal whose ROC is $\sigma>1$, decide whether the Fourier-transform slice $s=j\omega$ is included.

choice_blocks.text: Yes; the slice is included because $0>1$ is true.
No; the slice is not included because $s=j\omega$ gives $\sigma=0$ and $0>1$ is false.
Yes; the slice is included for all values of $\omega$ because the ROC condition should be checked with $\omega$.
No; the slice is excluded only because the ROC should be tested with $\sigma=\omega$.
Yes; every right-half-plane ROC automatically includes the Fourier-transform slice.

questions.correct_answer: No; since $s=j\omega$ has $\sigma=0$ and $0>1$ is false, the Fourier-transform slice is not included in the ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The Fourier-transform slice is the line $s=j\omega$, so its real part is $\sigma=0$. Substitute that value into the ROC inequality.
Because $\sigma=0$ does not satisfy the ROC, the $j\omega$ axis is not included and $X(j\omega)$ does not exist for this ROC.

prompt_blocks.text: For a signal whose ROC is $\sigma<0$, decide whether the Fourier-transform slice $s=j\omega$ is included.

choice_blocks.text: Yes; the slice is included because $0<0$ is true on the boundary.
Yes; the slice is included because strict ROC boundaries still contain the boundary line.
No; $s=j\omega$ gives $\sigma=0$, and $0<0$ is false.
No; the test should use $\omega<0$, so only negative frequencies converge.
Yes; the slice is included because the ROC points toward the left half-plane.

questions.correct_answer: No; $s=j\omega$ means $\sigma=0$, and $0<0$ is false, so the Fourier-transform slice is outside the ROC.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The inclusion test uses the real part of $s=j\omega$, not the value of $\omega$. On that slice, $\sigma=0$.
Since the inequality is strict, the boundary line $\sigma=0$ is not included. Therefore the Fourier-transform slice is not included in the ROC.
